analysis.one_liner: Ends a tax break for hardrock mining and puts part of the recovered money into cleaning up abandoned mines.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 7, 2005 and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Hardrock mining companies — gold, silver, copper and similar mines on federal and formerly federal land — can deduct a fixed percentage of their income as 'percentage depletion,' a tax break dating to older mining law. The bill would remove that deduction for these mines, raising federal revenue, and would direct a quarter of the new money into a trust fund to reclaim abandoned mines: sealing old mine openings, treating polluted mine drainage, and stabilizing eroding mine sites.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would no longer subsidize mining profits through the tax code; and communities near abandoned hardrock mines, whose lands and waterways would get a dedicated funding stream for reclamation — sealing mine entries, treating acid mine drainage, and controlling erosion and subsidence.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code to disallow the percentage depletion allowance for hardrock mines located on lands subject to the general mining laws or on land patented under them [S2] [S3].

It creates an Abandoned Mine Reclamation Trust Fund in the Treasury, funded with 25 percent of the added revenue from the repeal, for the Interior Secretary to spend on reclaiming abandoned mine areas, treating mine drainage pollution, replanting eroded land, and fixing subsidence from old deep mines [S2] [S3].
Eligible sites are abandoned or inadequately reclaimed lands in states subject to the general mining laws where no company retains reclamation responsibility under state or federal law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on public mining lands or lands patented under the general mining laws, which would lose a long-standing tax deduction and pay more in federal income taxes beginning with tax years after 2004.

drawbacks.text: The reclamation fund captures only 25 percent of the new revenue, leaving three quarters to general treasury purposes rather than mine cleanup [S3].
Sites already designated for cleanup under the uranium tailings law or listed for Superfund remediation are excluded from the fund [S3].

Removing the depletion deduction would raise costs for domestic hardrock producers; an honest supporter would acknowledge possible effects on mining jobs and output, though the bill's premise is that the deduction is a subsidy taxpayers should not carry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a straightforward tax-fairness change — ending a deduction available to hardrock miners but not to comparable industries — with a modest, self-funding cleanup program. Its main design limitation is that only a quarter of the recovered revenue goes to abandoned-mine reclamation, and the cleanup eligibility rules are narrow. On balance it is a well-targeted, low-cost reform whose benefits fall on taxpayers and mine-scarred communities, with the cost borne by a single industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Russell Feingold introduced the bill in the Senate on March 7, 2005 [S1] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on March 7, 2005; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S5] [S1].
The committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and the bill received no vote in either chamber before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies, which kept the percentage depletion deduction and avoided paying more in taxes; taxpayers and abandoned-mine communities gained nothing, since the reclamation fund was never created.

for.name: Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on March 7, 2005.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA) in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor action; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: Industry holding the percentage depletion deduction
against.what_they_did: No recorded activity on this bill, but the industry has long defended the depletion allowance in tax debates, and its benefit under current law continued.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; both of its sponsors were Democrats, while hardrock mining tax breaks have traditionally been defended by senators of both parties from mining states.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining (gold, silver, copper and other metal mines)
industries.note: The bill would end the percentage depletion deduction these companies claim on mines on public mining lands, costing them a long-standing tax subsidy; 25 percent of the recovered revenue would fund abandoned-mine cleanup. The industry retained the deduction because the bill died.

industries.industry: State and federal reclamation agencies and communities near abandoned mines
industries.note: The bill would have created a dedicated trust fund, financed by the repealed subsidy, for sealing old mine openings, treating mine drainage pollution, and restoring mined lands and waters. It was never funded.
